papers.title: Quantifying the extinction probability of Marburg virus disease outbreaks: A continuous-time Markov chain model integrating a multi-type branching process
papers.abstract: Understanding the extinction dynamics of Marburg virus disease is crucial, particularly during the early stages of an outbreak when stochastic effects strongly influence disease outcomes. Although deterministic models have provided valuable insights into virus transmission dynamics, they cannot adequately capture random transmission events or quantify extinction probabilities, particularly when outbreaks begin with few infected cases. This study develops a continuous-time Markov chain stochastic model derived from a deterministic multi-host transmission model. The model incorporates a multi-type branching process, in which distinct infectious types are tracked according to their contributions to secondary infections, enabling estimation of disease extinction probabilities during the early outbreak phase. The extinction analysis shows that outbreaks initiated by exposed humans have a higher probability of extinction (21.6%) compared with those initiated by infectious humans (13.7%), whereas outbreaks initiated by infected bats have an extinction probability of only 0.36%, highlighting their role as important reservoirs sustaining virus transmission. Furthermore, the results demonstrate that reducing human-to-human transmission, decreasing viral shedding, and increasing environmental viral decay significantly enhance the likelihood of disease extinction. The proposed framework provides a quantitative tool for assessing Marburg virus disease outbreak risk and valuable insights for designing early interventions for human transmission, environmental contamination, and cross-species interactions.

papers.title: Who leads Marburg virus research? Gender, geography and funding in authorship, 2008 to early 2023: a bibliometric baseline before the 2023-2025 outbreaks
papers.abstract: Between 2023 and 2025, Marburg virus disease reached Equatorial Guinea, Tanzania, Rwanda and Ethiopia for the first time. WHO's 2025 Marburg research priorities make leadership of studies by local scientists a continuing goal. This study describes who led Marburg virus research before these outbreaks. I analysed 684 English-language Web of Science papers on Marburg virus published from 2008 to February 2023 (5,700 authorships). Gender was inferred from first names with Gender-API, papers about African countries were identified from their text, funders were harmonised by country and type, and themes were mapped to the WHO priorities. I used Wilson 95% confidence intervals (CIs) and logistic and negative binomial regression. Women held 35.1% (95% CI 33.9-36.4) of authorships, 41.6% (37.9-45.4) of first-author and 19.6% (16.7-22.9) of last-author positions. Women last authors rose from 15.1% (2008-2012) to 23.2% (2018-2023). Only 14.6% of papers had an author based in Africa. Of 102 papers about an African country, 25.5% (18.0-34.7) had a first author and 23.5% (16.4-32.6) a last author from that country, below benchmarks for infectious-disease research in Africa. Women based in Africa were last author on 2 papers. Of funded papers, 69.0% acknowledged a US funder (24.0% a US defence agency) and 3.2% an African funder. WHO priorities on clinical care, outbreak trials, social science and capacity strengthening each appeared in fewer than 8% of papers. An apparent citation penalty for funded papers disappeared after adjustment (rate ratio 1.07, 0.87-1.33). Before the recent outbreaks, Marburg virus research was led mostly by men in senior positions and by researchers outside the affected countries, and was funded mainly by US agencies. This baseline can track whether recent African-led responses change who leads the field.

papers.title: Cross-reactive antibody and functional T-cell responses to Bundibugyo virus induced by Zaire ebolavirus vaccination and infection
papers.abstract: Background There is no licensed specific vaccine against the current Ebola Bundibugyo virus (BDBV) outbeak affecting the Democratic Republic of the Congo. However, clinical evaluations of a licensed Zaire ebolavirus (EBOV) vaccine have just launched. It remains unclear whether EBOV infection or vaccination generate cross-reactive immunity against BDBV. Methods We quantified CD4 and CD8 T-cell magnitude, polyfunctionality, and cytotoxicity after 8-day expansion with EBOV, BDBV, Sudan (SUDV), or Marburg (MARV) GP peptide pools, and measured GP-binding antibodies by multiplex assay, in recipients of Ad26.ZEBOV/MVA-BN-Filo (n=10), single-dose rVSVG-ZEBOV-GP (n=10), or two-dose rVSVG-ZEBOV-GP (n=8) (NCT02876328), and in EVD survivors sampled approximately 3 years after infection (n=10). Findings Fourteen days after completion of each licensed vaccine regimen, median BDBV-reactive CD4 responses were 9.8% [IQR:8.9-14.0] after single-dose rVSVG-ZEBOV-GP (D14) and 8.0% [5.5-9.9] after Ad26.ZEBOV/MVA-BN-Filo (D70). The highest BDBV-reactive CD8response was observed in survivors (24.7% [20.3-33.1]), together with a prominent cytotoxic CD8 response (14.4% [10.4-19.7]) ; corresponding vaccine-group medians ranged from 0.9% to 17.7% and from 0.6% to 6.7%, respectively. SUDV responses were also detected, whereas MARV recognition was limited. BDBV-binding antibodies were detected following both vaccine regimens, with the highest levels observed in survivors (491 [330-1261] net MFI). Among vaccinees, EBOV- and BDBV-reactive cellular and humoral responses were positively correlated after adjustment for multiple testing. Interpretation EBOV infection and vaccination elicited BDBV-cross-reactive T-cell responses and binding antibodies. These findings support further evaluation of existing EBOV vaccines in the context of BDBV outbreaks. Funding INSERM, Vaccine Research Institute (ANR-10-LABX-77-01), and Institut de Recherche pour le Developpement (IRD).

papers.source_body_en: Background There is no licensed specific vaccine against the current Ebola Bundibugyo virus (BDBV) outbeak affecting the Democratic Republic of the Congo. However, clinical evaluations of a licensed Zaire ebolavirus (EBOV) vaccine have just launched. It remains unclear whether EBOV infection or vaccination generate cross-reactive immunity against BDBV. Methods We quantified CD4 and CD8 T-cell magnitude, polyfunctionality, and cytotoxicity after 8-day expansion with EBOV, BDBV, Sudan (SUDV), or Marburg (MARV) GP peptide pools, and measured GP-binding antibodies by multiplex assay, in recipients of Ad26.ZEBOV/MVA-BN-Filo (n=10), single-dose rVSVG-ZEBOV-GP (n=10), or two-dose rVSVG-ZEBOV-GP (n=8) (NCT02876328), and in EVD survivors sampled approximately 3 years after infection (n=10). Findings Fourteen days after completion of each licensed vaccine regimen, median BDBV-reactive CD4 responses were 9.8% [IQR:8.9-14.0] after single-dose rVSVG-ZEBOV-GP (D14) and 8.0% [5.5-9.9] after Ad26.ZEBOV/MVA-BN-Filo (D70). The highest BDBV-reactive CD8response was observed in survivors (24.7% [20.3-33.1]), together with a prominent cytotoxic CD8 response (14.4% [10.4-19.7]) ; corresponding vaccine-group medians ranged from 0.9% to 17.7% and from 0.6% to 6.7%, respectively. SUDV responses were also detected, whereas MARV recognition was limited. BDBV-binding antibodies were detected following both vaccine regimens, with the highest levels observed in survivors (491 [330-1261] net MFI). Among vaccinees, EBOV- and BDBV-reactive cellular and humoral responses were positively correlated after adjustment for multiple testing. Interpretation EBOV infection and vaccination elicited BDBV-cross-reactive T-cell responses and binding antibodies. These findings support further evaluation of existing EBOV vaccines in the context of BDBV outbreaks. Funding INSERM, Vaccine Research Institute (ANR-10-LABX-77-01), and Institut de Recherche pour le Developpement (IRD).

papers.title: Mechanism of Action Studies of Small Molecule Entry Inhibitors Targeting Filovirus Glycoproteins
papers.abstract: Ebola virus (EBOV) and Marburg virus (MARV) are highly pathogenic filoviruses. Infection with either of these viruses results in viral hemorrhagic fever (VHF), a severe disease that can lead to multiorgan failure, internal bleeding, and, oftentimes, death. Currently, no antivirals are approved for the treatment of filoviruses, underscoring the urgent need for broad-spectrum antivirals. Currently, two vaccines are FDA-approved against EBOV disease; however, they are only effective against EBOV Zaire, while recent EBOV outbreaks have been caused by EBOV Sudan, underscoring the need for broad-spectrum vaccines and antivirals. Thus, our research goal is to develop small molecule inhibitors that directly target the filoviral glycoprotein (GP), which mediates viral entry into host cells for both EBOV and MARV. Our study is divided into two chapters: the development of broad-spectrum anti-filoviral entry inhibitors and the elucidation of the mechanisms of action (MOAs) of novel small molecule entry inhibitors.

Infection with either of these viruses results in viral hemorrhagic fever (VHF), a severe disease that can lead to multiorgan failure, internal bleeding, and, oftentimes, death. Currently, two vaccines are FDA-approved against EBOV disease; however, they are only effective against EBOV Zaire, while recent EBOV outbreaks have been caused by EBOV Sudan, underscoring the need for broad-spectrum vaccines and antivirals. Thus, our research goal is to develop small molecule inhibitors that directly target the filoviral glycoprotein (GP), which mediates viral entry into host cells for both EBOV and MARV. analysis_en.limitations_and_evidence_strength: The study is limited by its focus on a single outbreak, which may not be representative of all Marburg virus transmission scenarios. However, the evidence is strong given the detailed genetic and epidemiological analysis conducted.

analysis_zh.study_design_and_population: 该研究分析了埃塞俄比亚首个 暴发 和 马尔堡病毒病 的样本,重点关注 传播 模式和受影响人群中的病毒持续性。暴发 事件发生在特定地理位置,涉及人类 宿主。

PeriodDayWeek Company Profile Island Pharmaceuticals Limited is an Australia-based drug repurposing company. The Company is focused on areas of unmet need for antiviral therapeutics to address infectious diseases. Its lead asset is ISLA-101, a drug with a safety profile being repurposed for the prevention and treatment of dengue fever and other mosquito (or vector) borne diseases. ISLA-101 has been shown to have activity against all four strains of dengue virus as well as other flaviviruses such as Zika virus, West Nile virus, and Yellow Fever virus, as well as Chikungunya virus. While ISLA-101 is an oral formulation, the Company is also considering alternative formulations, including a long-acting oral formulation and intravenous formulations for severe dengue infections. The Company operates a single segment, being research and development activities principally in the geographic regions of Australia and the United States. Its subsidiary is Isla Pharmaceuticals Inc.
